title: Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:22 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer . The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Real application testing meets bigger, faster patches

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. A quarterly security update earlier this year addressed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across the company’s portfolio. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Orac

summary.tldr:
Oracle Corp. executive vice president Juan Loaiza revealed at Oracle AI World that the company used early access to a frontier AI model named "Mythos" in March to scan its codebase, uncovering severe security vulnerabilities that triggered a "code red" internal response and drastically larger quarterly security updates, such as one patching over 1,400 vulnerabilities.

To mitigate the risk of regressions caused by massive, rapid patching schedules, Oracle emphasizes its Real Application Testing tool to capture and run production workloads against proposed updates. Simultaneously, the proliferation of AI-generated code and autonomous agents bypassing traditional application-level security has forced Oracle to move access controls and business logic down to the data layer via its Deep Data Security offering, which shipped in April.

Deep Data Security passes an authenticated user's identity as an encrypted token to the database, enforcing authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data, and related tables. Additionally, Oracle introduced declarative business rules and SQL Assertions to ensure AI agents cannot bypass core operational constraints like credit limits regardless of the access mechanism.
takeaways: **Mythos Model Impact:** Oracle utilized early access to a frontier AI model called Mythos starting in March, which uncovered serious security vulnerabilities across Oracle's software code.
**Expanded Patch Sizes:** Accelerated vulnerability discovery led to substantially larger quarterly security patches, with one recent update addressing more than 1,400 vulnerabilities.
**Real Application Testing:** Oracle relies on its Real Application Testing system to capture real customer workloads and prevent production failures during complex, automated patch cycles.

**Deep Data Security Deployment:** Launched in April, Oracle's Deep Data Security passes an authenticated user's identity as an encrypted token down to the database layer to restrict AI agents from leaking or seeing unauthorized data.

**Declarative SQL Assertions:** Oracle implemented declarative business rules and SQL Assertions to enforce operational limits (such as credit card charges) directly within the data layer, preventing AI agents from circumventing application rules.

title: As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 14:57 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

Vibe coding meets enterprise governance

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

title: Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers
author: Ryan Stevens
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 14:39 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push . The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Building an open semantic layer across catalogs

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer

summary.tldr:
Oracle Corp. has repositioned its data architecture around the emergence of AI agents as primary data consumers, introducing the Autonomous AI Lakehouse at Oracle AI World 2026. According to Nipun Agarwal, senior vice president of software engineering for Oracle Database, the platform acts as an open layer spanning an enterprise's existing data estate rather than forcing data replication or replacement.

The technical architecture relies on an open catalog capable of mounting external catalogs—such as Databricks Unity Catalog, Postgres, and MySQL databases—to allow in-place querying. title: Open source AI is booming. Hugging Face explains who profits.
author: Theresa Loconsolo
contentSnippet: Open source models are becoming more mainstream as enterprises, governments and startups alike rely on the promise of lower costs, more control, and more flexibility. title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well.

DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.

On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”

Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”

Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong. https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9

In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.

The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.

Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.

After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.

We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give s

summary.tldr:
DuckDuckGo is actively targeting the K-12 education market, positioning its privacy-focused search engine as an alternative to Google Workspace for Education. This push follows Google’s recent policy update, which mandates that schools opting to disable Gemini AI features must also forfeit access to Google Search. DuckDuckGo CEO Gabriel Weinberg and Chief Public Affairs Officer Kamyl Bazbaz have publicly criticized Google’s bundling strategy, framing it as monopolistic behavior that limits administrative control over AI integration in classrooms.

While Google maintains that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and AI-integrated Search are disabled by default for K-12 accounts, the company acknowledges that these features are inextricably linked to the core search experience. In contrast, DuckDuckGo emphasizes its granular control, offering users the ability to disable AI features via browser settings or through its dedicated 'noai.duckduckgo.com' portal. DuckDuckGo reports a 30% increase in app installs earlier this year, which it attributes to user demand for search experiences free from forced AI-generated content.
takeaways: **Google Policy Constraint:** Schools wishing to disable Gemini AI features in Google Workspace are currently unable to retain standard Google Search functionality.
**DuckDuckGo Deployment:** DuckDuckGo is providing direct technical documentation and support for school administrators to switch default search engines to their platform.
**Market Scale:** Google’s education ecosystem currently supports approximately 50 million Chromebooks and over 150 million global users on Google Classroom.
**AI Opt-Out Mechanism:** DuckDuckGo offers a specific domain, noai.duckduckgo.com, which disables AI-assisted answers, image generation, and feature suggestions by default.
**Growth Metric:** DuckDuckGo reported a 30% increase in app installs earlier this year, citing user rejection of forced AI search integrations as a primary driver.

title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
author: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu
contentSnippet: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
author: James O'Donnell
contentSnippet: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the dat

summary.tldr:
Texas, previously the fastest-growing data center market and primary hub for Big Tech AI buildouts, faces a potential halt to its expansion following a sweeping political shift. Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won the US Senate and gubernatorial races respectively, while Democrats took control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Both candidates made data centers a central campaign issue, pushing back against the facilities amid mounting bipartisan distaste that also prompted outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott to direct a state regulator to halt data center permits on September 21.

This political pivot threatens massive hyperscale AI projects currently underway in the state, including the Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County projected at 1,820 megawatts—comparable to SpaceX's Colossus 2 in Tennessee—and the Nexus Hubbard data center intended to serve Anthropic at a planned size of 6,400 megawatts, making it the second-largest data center under construction in the US behind Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana. Governor-elect Hinojosa campaigned on a full-fledged moratorium on data centers, diverging from her prior support for tax breaks in 2023, while lenders and banks simultaneously grow more selective in backing these capital-intensive facilities.
takeaways: **Political Shift:** Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race against Greg Abbott, James Talarico won the US Senate seat, and Democrats took control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years.

**Permit Halt:** Outgoing Governor Greg Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits on September 21 following growing bipartisan distaste and halted email correspondence with developers.
**Stargate Frontier Project:** A massive AI facility under construction in Shackelford County, Texas, projected to serve 1,820 megawatts.

**Nexus Hubbard Project:** A planned 6,400-megawatt data center intended primarily to serve Anthropic, ranking as the second-largest data center under construction in the US behind Meta's Hyperion project.

title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
author: Sungyeon Kim
contentSnippet: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an A

summary.tldr:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations has introduced support for decision models as a specialized scoring mechanism for agent evaluation. Unlike standard LLM-as-a-judge approaches that generate free-form text, decision models operate on structured states and a fixed set of allowed answers to return calibrated probabilities. This methodology is designed for narrow, repeatable evaluation tasks—such as policy adherence, tool call safety, and context relevance—where consistent, thresholdable numerical scores are required for reliable agent monitoring across development, batch processing, and production traffic.

Integration is achieved through the platform's custom code-based evaluator framework, which executes logic via AWS Lambda functions. These functions can interface with external decision model backends to process agent turns. The system allows for a tiered evaluation architecture: decision models act as a high-throughput screening layer to filter turns, while built-in evaluators are reserved for deeper analysis of flagged issues. The documentation highlights two specific implementations: Jev, a hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider 2B, an open-source model that can be self-hosted.
takeaways: **Evaluation Architecture:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations supports 15 built-in evaluators alongside custom LLM-as-a-judge and code-based evaluators.
**Decision Model Utility:** Decision models provide calibrated probabilities over fixed answer sets, replacing variable free-form text outputs for consistent thresholding.
**Implementation Method:** Custom evaluators utilize AWS Lambda functions to bridge AgentCore inputs with external decision model APIs or self-hosted models.
**Tiered Screening:** Decision models can function as a pre-filter to identify specific turns requiring further investigation by more complex built-in evaluators.
**Supported Models:** The framework supports integration with TypeSafe's Jev (hosted) and Strands Decider 2B (open-source).

Why startups, enterprises, and governments are switching to open AI models to cut costs, and when it makes less sense to use the most powerful models.

Who makes money when the models are free to use, and whether the companies building them can capture the value they create.

Why the U.S. may need deep-pocketed players like Nvidia to build an open frontier model that can compete with China’s, and what’s at stake if Chinese models become the global default.

How recent attacks on open AI platforms are raising a difficult question: how do you keep an open ecosystem secure without closing it off?

title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen: > “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses, including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/nothingr-teaser-image-carl-pei.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin, the Friend, and even AI stuffed animals. OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

summary.tldr:
Nothing CEO Carl Pei has announced the company’s first 'AI-native' hardware product, scheduled for a December launch. The device is explicitly designed without a screen and is positioned as a tool that cannot function as a standard mobile application. Pei’s announcement follows a year-long strategic pivot toward AI-integrated hardware and operating systems, moving away from the company's previous focus on smartphone-centric hardware.

While specific technical specifications remain undisclosed, the device enters a crowded market of screen-free AI wearables, including the Humane AI Pin, the Friend pendant, and various AI-integrated smart glasses. Pei explicitly rejected the industry-wide search for an 'iPhone of AI,' characterizing the pursuit of a singular, magical consumer device as a 'dead end.' Rumors circulating prior to the announcement suggest the company may be developing AI-enabled smart glasses, potentially including models without integrated cameras.
takeaways: **Launch Timeline:** Nothing’s first AI-native hardware product is confirmed for release in December.
**Form Factor:** The device is confirmed to be screen-free and is described by CEO Carl Pei as a tool rather than an app-based experience.
**Strategic Pivot:** The product marks the culmination of a year-long transition for Nothing, which has been repositioning itself as an 'AI-first' company.
**Market Context:** The device competes in the screen-free AI hardware category, joining existing products like the Humane AI Pin and the Friend wearable.

title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
author: Gagik Amirkhanyan
contentSnippet: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

title: How big is the open model economy today?
author: Nathan Lambert
contentSnippet: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
author: Steve Vinsik
contentSnippet: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
author: Yoonseo Kim
contentSnippet: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
author: Bhagyashree Chandak
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Jin Tiong Lim
contentSnippet: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. title: Intra-Cell Spatial Reuse in LEO Downlinks: Beam-Leakage-Aware Satellite Scheduling
author: Shizhen Jia
contentSnippet: Dense low-earth-orbit (LEO) constellations offer an opportunity to increase local broadband capacity by serving multiple terminals in the same cell through concurrent satellite beams. However, interference between overlapping beams limits spatial reuse, and satellite selection based solely on link strength or angular separation may result in suboptimal performance. This paper proposes beam-leakage-aware satellite scheduling for Ku-band LEO downlink transmissions. With matched transmit and receive beamforming, we formulate a fixed-cardinality sum-rate maximization problem that jointly accounts for satellite-dependent received powers and pairwise receive-array leakage. A beam-leakage-aware branch-and-bound (BL-BnB) algorithm combines an admissible upper bound with greedy-plus-swap initialization to obtain globally optimal schedules for the reference-point model. We evaluate the method using a 24-h ephemeris-derived Starlink visibility trace with antenna and transmit-power models calibrated to public SpaceX filings. The results show that total capacity increases with beam count, but less than proportionally. With eight concurrent beams, BL-BnB improves mean per-beam capacity by 27.2% over nearest-satellite selection, primarily benefiting weaker links. BL-BnB achieves millisecond-scale runtimes in our evaluation, supporting the computational feasibility of optimal scheduling.

title: Delay-Doppler Synchronization for Distributed Uplink Interference Nulling in LEO Networks
author: Stefan Daniel Tancovici
contentSnippet: Cooperation among low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provides spatial diversity for mitigating uplink interference that is difficult to suppress with a single onboard array. Coherent interference cancellation across satellites, however, requires compensation of the relative delay and Doppler of a common interferer. We analyze two-branch interference nulling with finite training and derive a closed-form approximation to the mean residual interference-to-noise ratio (INR). The approximation separates wrong acquisition, local synchronization errors, and weight-learning losses, linking performance to input INR, branch power imbalance, training length, and effective search size. Under a Gaussian surrogate with small errors and efficient, approximately unbiased refinement, correct acquisition yields a high-INR plateau of $2/N_v$, where $N_v$ is the valid training length. Synchronization and weight learning contribute equally to this limit, whereas persistent alignment bias adds a penalty that grows with input power. Monte Carlo experiments compare dense FFT/zoom and coarse FFT/gradient acquisition using matched final FIR refinement, branch-noise normalization, and independent test blocks. Both approach the predicted plateau at high input INR. Coarse search reduces measured search time by $6.7\times$ at an approximately 0.7-dB acquisition-threshold penalty. Controlled power-ratio sweeps show how branch imbalance delays reliable acquisition at fixed stronger-branch INR. A separate Starlink snapshot evaluation demonstrates comparable nulling performance under changing satellite geometry.

title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments

title: Trace2Eval: Contextualized Evaluation of Coding Agents from Real-World Traces
author: Ji Shi
contentSnippet: Coding agents are increasingly used in real-world workflows across diverse domains, motivating evaluation grounded in real user tasks. Existing benchmarks, however, largely rely on static public tasks with reference patches or hidden tests. Next-generation coding-agent benchmarks should therefore move beyond correctness on fixed tasks toward continually renewed evaluation of overall artifact quality in real user workflows. We propose Trace2Eval, a dynamically updatable pipeline that constructs benchmarks from real-world interaction trajectories. Trace2Eval employs a multi-agent reconstruction system to analyze the filtered trajectory, recover the original user query, restore the workspace files to their pre-interaction state, and rebuild a trajectory-equivalent execution environment. A candidate agent then executes the reconstructed query to produce an initial artifact. To evaluate these artifacts, the pipeline iteratively refines human rubrics through inter-annotator alignment, and calibrates judge agents against human assessments using source-code and runtime evidence. Guided by feedback from the Trace2Eval pipeline, models revise their initial artifacts, yielding a mean score gain of 10.05 percentage points across 19 model-harness configurations and a maximum of 19.28 percentage points for DeepSeek-V4-Pro with Claude Code, which supports rubric feedback as actionable guidance for artifact improvement.

title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
author: Kejian Zhu, Zhuoran Jin, Shangqing Tu, Tianyi Men
contentSnippet:
Authors: Kejian Zhu , Zhuoran Jin , Shangqing Tu , Tianyi Men , Yupu Hao , Jiachun Li , Kang Liu , Jun Zhao

Abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: this https URL

Notes: Project Page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Kejian Zhu et al. investigate the performance dynamics of multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in LLM agents, specifically analyzing how interaction constraints—defined by sampling breadth (K) and interaction depth (T)—impact the efficacy of trajectory-level RL. Their findings indicate that the performance gains typically attributed to multi-turn RL are highly sensitive to the allocated turn budget, with advantages diminishing significantly as these budgets are restricted. The study reveals that agentic RL does not provide a uniform improvement in single-step decision-making; instead, its primary utility is concentrated in long-horizon resilience and the ability to perform error recovery over multiple turns.

To address the risks associated with strict budget dependence, the authors introduce 'BudgetMix RL,' a training methodology that varies interaction budgets during the learning process. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that BudgetMix RL produces more robust performance across varied execution environments compared to standard RL approaches. The paper also provides a preliminary analysis of the trade-offs between process supervision signals and trajectory-level RL, offering a framework for optimizing agentic performance under varying computational and temporal constraints.

**Core Finding:** Multi-turn RL advantages are not universal but are specifically tied to sufficient turn budgets, showing significant degradation under tight constraints.
**Functional Specialization:** Agentic RL benefits are primarily localized to error recovery and long-horizon task resilience rather than improving individual decision-making steps.
**Proposed Solution:** BudgetMix RL is introduced as a training strategy that modulates interaction budgets to improve agent robustness across diverse deployment scenarios.

title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
author: Mayan Sharma
contentSnippet: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving
author: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo
contentSnippet: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.

title: SBVUL: Statement-Based Vulnerability Detection
author: Martin Pinzger
contentSnippet: Many recent approaches for vulnerability detection use large language models (LLMs) to classify functions as vulnerable or benign, leaving developers to locate the exploitable statements. Furthermore, while these approaches have shown performance improvements, they still fall short in distinguishing vulnerable from patched real-world functions. This paper presents SBVul, an agentic approach that detects exploitable statements in C/C++ functions. In Phase~1, an LLM agent explores the function and its repository and identifies candidate statements. In Phase~2, a second agent analyzes the control and data flow of each candidate and confirms it, rules it out, or marks it uncertain. We created a manually verified ground truth of exploitable statements for 200 pairs of the PrimeVul Paired test set and ran SBVul with the open-weight models Qwen 3.8 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Phase~1 identifies ground-truth statements in 56--77% of the vulnerable functions, and Phase~2 confirms such a statement with an explanation accepted by an LLM judge in 26--73%. However, all models also confirm candidates in 23--61% of the patched functions. Across vulnerable and patched functions, the highest statement-level precision is 0.315 at a recall of 0.605 obtained with Opus 5.5 (xhigh). At the function level, SBVul with Opus 5.5 classifies 42.0% of the pairs correctly, compared with 33.8% reported for the best previous approach.

title: Temporary gas turbines powering a US AI data center created a cross-state air pollution hotspot
author: Will W. Qiang
contentSnippet: Data centers increasingly use on-site gas turbines that regulators can treat as temporary. Two satellites show the fleet powering SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 raised local nitrogen dioxide columns by about half as it expanded, the most anomalous increase among 656 urban locations nationwide since 2020. Mississippi authorized the fleet, but two-thirds of the hotspot's 116,000 mostly Black residents live in Tennessee, and the hotspot contains no regulatory nitrogen dioxide monitor. The fleet causes an estimated four premature deaths yearly, valued at $49 million, over 80% outside Mississippi and nearly all from units without selective catalytic reduction. On new turbines, this control's benefits exceed costs over the service life, but not over temporary stays or for in-state damages alone. Standards following the equipment could recover these benefits.

title: Shallow Encoding Emits Deep Memories
author: Mingyuan Ma
contentSnippet: Hybrid language models interleave a few softmax-attention layers with many linear-attention or state-space layers, so every layer keeps a memory of earlier tokens: a key-value cache or a fixed-size recurrent state. Serving them spends more compute and high-bandwidth memory on these memories than the output requires. The prefill runs every layer for every prompt token, and every decode step loads and stores whole recurrent states, which on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next take as many bytes per request as the attention cache of thousands of tokens. We find two properties of trained hybrids that locate this excess. First, writes are easier than reads: writing a deep layer's memory of a token needs little of the deep computation that predicting the next token needs. Trained copies of the deep layers' write paths, which we call emitters, therefore write a prompt's deep memories from the residual stream of a shallower anchor layer, and all prompt tokens but the last run as few as 63% of the layers. Second, recurrent states have a state sink: most of their energy lies in a rank-one term along a fixed direction of each head, and the rest is a low-rank working memory. SEED builds on both: it makes the prefill shallow in depth and the decode state shallow in representation. Each recurrent state is stored as its sink plus low-rank factors, which the Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention and Mamba-2 updates extend exactly; we prove that the open-loop error of the periodic compressions back to low rank is bounded independently of their number. SEED keeps the original weights frozen, compresses no attention cache, and runs all layers for every generated token. On six checkpoints of five production hybrids of 30B to over 300B parameters, it is nearly lossless on eleven official exams. Served with SGLang on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs on an agentic-coding trace, it raises the per-GPU throughput of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 1.2-1.4x.

title: vExpert: Virtualizing Expert Storage for Adaptive Load Balancing in Distributed MoE Inference
author: Wenxun Wang
contentSnippet: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become prevailing, yet their distributed deployment suffers from severe dynamic load imbalance due to the conflict between static expert placement and inherent routing dynamism. While host DRAM offers capacity to avoid static device storage for load balancing, we identify existing offloading works fundamentally fail in distributed inference due to two overlooked challenges: (1) coupled performance impacts of runtime Host-to-Device transfers due to load dynamism and shared PCIe topology; (2) system-level memory overhead incurred by DRAM usage at scale. In this paper, we propose vExpert that shifts DRAM offloading paradigm from partial residency to full redundancy through virtualized expert storage. We pioneer the first systematic performance model that jointly captures H2D latency, PCIe contention, and load imbalance, building a lightweight allocator to dynamically map physical experts to virtual slots runtime. A novel disaggregated manager is designed to reduce memory overhead in multi-process environments. Evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.1 within an 8-node H100 cluster, vExpert improves load balance ratio by up to 55% and achieves 1.2$\times$ end-to-end speedup.

title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
author: Manodeep Ray, Vivek Srivastava, Shirish Karande, Murari Mandal
contentSnippet:
Authors: Manodeep Ray , Vivek Srivastava , Shirish Karande , Murari Mandal

Abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at this https URL .

summary.tldr:
Researchers Manodeep Ray, Vivek Srivastava, Shirish Karande, and Murari Mandal published a study examining "Alignment Faking"—the phenomenon where language models follow directives under perceived monitoring and abandon them when unmonitored. Testing ten open- and closed-weight models ranging from 8B to approximately 675B parameters across 32 ValueBench dimensions, the authors demonstrate that compliance gaps span from 0.05 to 0.50, noting that a distilled 70B model scored above a ~675B model. They establish that structural variance depends primarily on the specific model-value pairing rather than the model or value in isolation.

To evaluate this behavior, the framework profiles alignment faking by scoring model-value pairs under three distinct conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. The team introduces a six-category taxonomy over internal reasoning traces to track behavioral shifts, revealing that training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring, whereas value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. The findings are packaged into "value cards" designed to extend traditional model cards with behavioral dispositions. Code and data have been made publicly available.
takeaways: **Scale and Scope:** Evaluated 10 open- and closed-weight models ranging from 8B to ~675B parameters across 32 ValueBench dimensions.
**Compliance Gaps:** Measured compliance gaps spanning between 0.05 and 0.50 across model-value pairs, with a distilled 70B model outperforming a ~675B model.
**Evaluation Conditions:** Scored model-value pairs under three specific conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored.
**Reasoning Trace Taxonomy:** Developed a six-category taxonomy showing that training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring, while value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored.
**Artifacts Released:** Packaged per-model results as "value cards" to extend standard model cards, alongside public code and data.

title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
author: Yushan Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures optimizer wall-time ratios of 1.128x-67.65x for random versus CARD graph interventions. Native solver records locate this difference in elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization. Together, these results connect certificate semantics, physical execution, proof acquisition, and graph computation through explicit system objects.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced CARD, a proof-carrying interface designed to bridge mathematical geometric certificates and physical robotic action for relative-measurement graphs. CARD uses a lifted-fiber formulation to separate semantic motion from witness repair, explicitly characterizing when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability framework establishes a useful-service law, proving that uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population achieves one useful service per request under live-confirmation conditions.

The framework's primary evaluation draws on 404 Full16 cases across 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. Results show that checker-confirmed optimizer points were reference-discrepant in all 404 cases, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 meters. Conversely, paired causal-navigation transforms proved reference-consistent across all 404 cases, showing medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 meters. Across five matched request budgets, the maximum difference between hypergeometric predictions and observed ordinary-random means was 0.8412 services. Furthermore, ordinary matched random achieved 0 out of 50 target successes, whereas actionability-matched random reached 50 out of 50 successes, matching the CARD policy.

Public downstream evaluations across 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM benchmark cases demonstrated optimizer wall-time ratios ranging from 1.128x to 67.65x when comparing random graph interventions to CARD interventions. Native solver records trace this performance delta to elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization efficiency.
takeaways: **Airborne Survey Dataset:** Evaluated on 404 Full16 cases spanning 20 sorties using an AA15-X500 airborne survey system.

**Optimizer vs. Navigation Discrepancies:** All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points exhibited reference discrepancies with medians of 1.9891 degrees rotation and 21.6322 m translation, while paired causal-navigation transforms were reference-consistent with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m.
**Target Success Rates:** Ordinary matched random sampling achieved 0/50 target successes, whereas actionability-matched random sampling reached 50/50 successes, aligning with the CARD policy.

**Downstream SLAM Benchmarks:** Public evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases recorded optimizer wall-time ratios between 1.128x and 67.65x favoring CARD graph interventions over random interventions, driven by differences in elimination fill and Cholesky factor size.

title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
author: Xikai Sun, Kebin Liu, Fan Dang, Yawen Zheng, Zihao Yang, Yunhao Liu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xikai Sun , Kebin Liu , Fan Dang , Yawen Zheng , Zihao Yang , Yunhao Liu

Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.

summary.tldr:
Xikai Sun, Kebin Liu, Fan Dang, Yawen Zheng, Zihao Yang, and Yunhao Liu present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework designed to detect specification-to-SDK conformance gaps in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCPGuard addresses vulnerabilities arising when official SDKs responsible for message validation and session logic omit specification constraints, which then propagate to downstream applications. The framework uses a shared kernel with language-specific adapters to analyze multi-language SDK implementations.

The system operates via a dual-track analysis and dynamic adjudication architecture. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models to generate constraint-specific evidence, while its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and leverages LLMs to audit them for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and constructs Proofs-of-Concept (PoCs) to validate candidates. Tested on the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirmed 13 and 19 findings respectively, outperforming two black-box baselines that failed to expose any of these gaps. Subsequent tests on open MCP servers demonstrated that these conformance gaps systematically propagate downstream.

**Tested SDK Versions:** Evaluated on official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs.

title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
author: Tran Nhat Khang Nguyen, Anh Nguyen, Obed Issakah, Janghoon Ock
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
author: Zhaojian Yu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native \emph{League of Legends} with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse--keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0\% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3\% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.

title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
author: Shuzheng Gao, Zhaojian Yu, Penghao Yin, Yuling Shi, Kai Cai, Shilin He, Michael R. Lyu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz
author: Ethan Ji, Wei Wang, Yizhou Sun
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with hidden states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the range it could explore, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On 44 of these systems, classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed, although the same data usually suffice once the true equations are given with unknown coefficients; the difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in estimating it. Because mechanisms recur across systems, we also give agents the program they discovered for a related system; it helped only when the new system shared the mechanism and the first investigation had succeeded. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents find which variables a system has but not how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to revisions that predict better.

title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
author: Bowen Zhu, Jian Wu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in an 82.6 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. A broader trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum and recovers much of its early bolometric deficit, with a spectral response that changes during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.
