title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
author: YuJie Liu, Dezhen Xue, Jun Sun, Xiangdong Ding, Zhibin Gao, Turab Lookman
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
author: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

title: Probabilistic Steering of Generative Priors for Lab-in-the-Loop Antibody Optimization
author: Anisha Parsan, Sebastian Ober, Calvin McCarter, Nick Bhattacharya, Hunter Elliott
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Therapeutic antibody development is often framed as comprising two discrete stages: initial discovery of novel binders followed by iterative optimization to refine these hits into therapeutic-grade molecules. Models and methods often reflect these stages, with generative structure models applied to discovery and probabilistic black-box optimization methods applied to refinement. Here we propose to unify these stages by smoothly transitioning a generative discovery model into iterative optimization, allowing the handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet lab data to be guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. We show that this yields improvements in optimization efficiency in the low-N regime, as well as improved diversity amongst the optimized molecules.

title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models
author: Farid Hasanov, Riccardo Renzulli, Bahram Zonooz, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Decebal Constantin Mocanu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.

title: ExaTune: Exhaustive Hyperparameter Landscape Exploration at Scale
author: Kevin Dick, Katie Lonsway
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.03867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns a single optimal configuration, systematically discarding the explored performance landscape that encodes how results depend on configuration choices. Fitness landscape analysis comprises a robust collection of methods from evolutionary computation offering ruggedness indices, autocorrelation functions, and fitness-distance correlation that have never been applied to machine learning hyperparameter spaces at scale, given that fine-grained ground-truth enumeration data has not existed. We present ExaTune, an open-source HPC system to produce a new artifact class: the hyperparameter landscape map. ExaTune exhaustively evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid via $K$-fold cross-validation, aggregates results into reproducible parquet benchmarks, and applies a suite of five formalized landscape metrics: spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$), ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation (FDC), and variance-based parameter importance. We release a benchmark collection of 8 complete landscape maps (totalling 285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations) spanning five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression, and $k$-nearest neighbors) across six classification and two regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Empirical analysis demonstrates that Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband, and Random Search at standard trial budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interaction effects that are visible in complete landscapes; information that is structurally unavailable to any optimizer by design.

title: Tencent WeVisOne-VL Unifies Detection, OCR, Segmentation and Matting
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Tencent’s WeChat Vision team has released WeVisOne-VL , an open vision language model in 2B and 4B sizes. The WeVisOne-VL vision language model handles detection, referring, counting, pointing, OCR, segmentation and alpha matting in one model. Pixel outputs come from a 9.6M-parameter decoder, so no separate SAM is needed. It also answers “None” when a queried object is absent. For developers, that can replace a detector, an OCR engine and a segmenter with one model. TL;DR Size: 2B ( 2.44B params ) and 4B ( 4.83B params ) on Hugging Face, and a 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder. Trained with up to 8,192 tokens of context; deployment context length is not disclosed. Runs on: A single GPU through Transformers or vLLM in BF16. The package also lists NPU and CPU devices. VRAM needs are not disclosed. A community GGUF ran object-level tasks on a 6 GB RTX 2060. Performance: Beats the same-scale VLM baselines in Tencent’s tables on most of 30+ benchmarks (self-reported). Best: 71.3 F1 Mean on Dense200 dense detection, versus 58.7 for LocateAnything-3B. Worst: 52.6% rejection rate on PR-Bench, so many absent-target queries still get a box. What is WeVisOne-VL? WeVisOne-VL (“WeChat Vision All-in-One”) is a perception-focused model from Tencent built on Qwen3-VL . It targets fine-grained localization rather than open-ended chat. Users choose the output granularity: points, boxes, binary masks or continuous alpha mattes. How does WeVisOne-VL work? Every task is cast as structured next-token prediction. The model adds coordinate tokens <0> to <1000> for normalized boxes and points. An absent target produces None instead of a guessed box. For pixel tasks, the model emits an <OBJ> token after each predicted box. Its hidden state becomes a query for the pixel decoder, according to the model card . Box-Guided Query Decoder: 6 deformable cross-attention blocks seeded by the <OBJ> state and the box. Dense Prediction Head: refines output at S/4, S/2 and S/1 into a full-resolution mask or matte. title: StarWorld: A Cross-Layer World Model for Starlink Prediction and Streaming
author: Bowen Zhang
contentSnippet: Starlink and other low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband systems exhibit stochastic access dynamics whose effects propagate from network measurements to throughput prediction and adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming, making reasoning over multiple plausible futures essential. Existing studies mainly characterize realized traces or individual system layers, leaving cross-layer world modeling of these evolving dynamics largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose StarWorld, a cross-layer world model for Starlink prediction and streaming. StarWorld couples learned stochastic network dynamics with executable prediction, control, and playback processes to imagine multi-step cross-layer futures, while a calibrated Trust Gate determines whether these futures are sufficiently reliable for use. On real Starlink measurements, StarWorld achieves the lowest network-future distributional errors among the comparison methods at the principal horizons and reduces pairwise controller quality-of-experience (QoE) effect error by 76%. These results support StarWorld as a cross-layer imagination environment for studying prediction and streaming outcomes under uncertain Starlink access conditions.

StarWorld couples learned stochastic network dynamics with executable prediction, control, and playback processes to imagine multi-step cross-layer futures, while a calibrated Trust Gate determines whether these futures are sufficiently reliable for use. On real Starlink measurements, StarWorld achieves the lowest network-future distributional errors among the comparison methods at the principal horizons and reduces pairwise controller quality-of-experience (QoE) effect error by 76%. These results support StarWorld as a cross-layer imagination environment for studying prediction and streaming outcomes under uncertain Starlink access conditions.

title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation
author: Harshit Gupta
contentSnippet: This study investigates the authorship impersonation capacity of six widely used large language models (LLMs): Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast. The evaluation was conducted using short product review texts selected to ensure high within author consistency in individual writing style. Two types of in context prompt were designed: a simple prompt with minimal instruction and a complex prompt incorporating explicit stylometric guidance for mimicry. Authorship mimicry was evaluated using a cosine distance based distance to training metric, supplemented by visual analyses of embedding distributions. The results indicate that authorship impersonation remained challenging for most LLMs, with Gemini 3 Pro showing the strongest apparent mimicry performance. However, subsequent overlap analysis revealed that Gemini 3 Pro extensively copied and reused sentences and phrases from the training texts, at levels far exceeding those observed among human authors. Follow up factor analyses showed that training set consistency was the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, whereas author distinctiveness did not generalise as a reliable predictor. Global embedding visualisations further revealed a consistent macro level pattern: for most models, generated texts occupied regions of the embedding space that were largely separated from the corresponding human training clusters. This indicates limited convergence towards target author style and suggests the presence of model specific lexical and phraseological preferences. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine stylistic imitation from direct textual reuse and have implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence involving potential LLM enabled impersonation.

title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
author: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao
contentSnippet:
Authors: Shuai Dong , Kanghui Tian , Linghan Chen , Wenqi Shao , Hongrui Wu , Haowen Hou , Yongfu Zhu , Xuehui Wang , Ziyue Wang , Wenpu Liu , Weichu Xie , Yuqi Xu , Congcong Wang , Kaiwen Tuo , Caoyuan Ma , Taiqiang Wu , Ji Zhao , Wenzheng Chang , Dianyi Wang , Siyuan Wang , Zhongyu Wei , Yu Qiao , Jiaqi Wang

Abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

Notes: 16 pages, 4 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers from Shanghai AI Lab and Fudan University have introduced TurnWise, a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize streaming video understanding models. The method addresses the limitations of standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which typically applies a single trajectory-level advantage across all turns. By decoupling credit assignment, TurnWise allows models to better evaluate individual decisions—specifically whether to respond or continue observing—thereby reducing redundant outputs and encouraging necessary follow-ups.

The technical architecture of TurnWise centers on two primary mechanisms: silence-completed prefix scoring and turn-mean policy optimization. The former constructs group-relative advantages based on the remaining return of each specific decision, effectively isolating the learning signal from historical rewards. The latter averages token losses within each turn and subsequently across turns, ensuring that 'respond' and 'wait' decisions are weighted equally regardless of the length of the generated output. This approach achieves performance gains without the need for a learned critic or additional rollouts, as detailed in the 16-page paper.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** TurnWise utilizes turn-level credit assignment to align reinforcement learning with individual streaming decisions in video understanding tasks.
**Credit Assignment:** The framework employs silence-completed prefix scoring to separate learning signals from earlier trajectory rewards.
**Optimization Strategy:** Turn-mean policy optimization balances the weight of 'respond' and 'wait' decisions by averaging token losses within and across turns.
**Efficiency:** The proposed method improves streaming policy learning without requiring a learned critic or additional rollout samples.
**Research Scope:** The study is documented in a 16-page paper featuring 4 figures and a 23-author research team.

title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
author: Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou
contentSnippet: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
author: Bingran You, Wenjun Ke, Ria Rosenauer, Bo Liu
contentSnippet: AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
author: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
contentSnippet: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?
author: Peiran Wu, Fangfei Gou, Zhaoxi Mu, Changhao Zhang
contentSnippet: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: 75.0%, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with 77.8%; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.

title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
author: Mohammad Reza Rezaei
contentSnippet: Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. We propose PAYWORTHY which contains 1{,}494 real freelance job postings, sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. We ask 18 models to forecast how likely the agent is to succeed and measure how well each model's forecasts rank the accepted jobs above the rejected ones (AUC, where 0.5 is a random ranking). The answer depends on how the agent is described. Told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs well (AUC 0.66--0.86). Told instead that it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank the same jobs about as well as a random ordering (0.45--0.56). These results hold under judges from four other model families (Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen), and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Payworthy

title: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
author: Elizabeth Lopatto
contentSnippet: People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows. What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.” The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds, on top of its existing steep commitments. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds, for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them. The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion. I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds, meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt. It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal, is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expect

summary.tldr:
Emmanuel Roman, CEO of PIMCO, has publicly warned of an impending downturn in the AI market, citing the massive debt load required to sustain the current infrastructure buildout. Roman estimates that AI development will necessitate $2 trillion in financing over the next five years, a significant figure relative to the $12 trillion total US bond market. Despite these warnings, demand for AI-related debt remains high; Meta recently attracted $58 billion in orders for a bond offering expected to range between $15 billion and $20 billion. Other major tech firms are similarly active in debt markets, with Oracle seeking $20 billion, Alphabet issuing €6 billion ($6.7 billion), and Microsoft recently selling $25 billion in bonds.

Financial institutions are showing signs of divergence regarding AI risk. While PIMCO has been a key financier of the AI trade—including early CoreWeave chip-based financing and significant holdings in Meta and SpaceX debt—its leadership is now signaling caution. Apollo Global Management, which has discussed a potential $40 billion chip deal with SpaceX, has also expressed uncertainty regarding the long-term pricing and economic viability of AI infrastructure. Potential catalysts for a market correction, according to Roman, include US rate hikes, geopolitical conflict, or a eurozone crisis, though the high volume of interest in recent bond offerings suggests the market has not yet reached a definitive peak.
takeaways: **Financing Scale:** PIMCO estimates the AI infrastructure buildout will require $2 trillion in financing over the next five years.
**Recent Debt Issuances:** Major tech firms have recently tapped debt markets, including Meta ($15B-$20B target), Oracle ($20B), Alphabet (€6B), and Microsoft ($25B).
**PIMCO's Market Position:** PIMCO previously realized $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds and recently purchased $4 billion in SpaceX debt.
**Institutional Caution:** Apollo Global Management president Jim Zelter cited significant uncertainty regarding how AI pricing and economics will evolve despite long-term demand for computing power.
**Market Triggers:** PIMCO CEO Emmanuel Roman identified US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers for an AI market correction.

title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
author: Russell Brandom
contentSnippet:
Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using.

Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results.

FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?”

To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device.

As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab.

“This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has introduced FlashProve, an open-source research project designed to provide "provable inference" for AI models. The system utilizes cryptographic proofs to verify that a specific AI model generated a particular output, ensuring that users can confirm the provenance of AI-generated content. By requiring labs to publish a "fingerprint" of their models, FlashProve allows for verification without exposing the model's proprietary weights, making it compatible with closed-source commercial models.

The technical architecture is designed to be lightweight, enabling verification to occur on local devices. The system aims to mitigate "model swapping," where providers might secretly substitute a cheaper or less capable model for a premium one, or falsely claim that a task was performed by a frontier-level model. The researchers have released the technical specification and working code on GitHub under an open-source license.

Currently, FlashProve is in the intermediate research phase, and Anthropic has no immediate plans to deploy the system within its own production environment. The company is positioning this as a collaborative effort, inviting the broader research community to iterate on the existing codebase and cryptographic framework.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** FlashProve provides a cryptographic guarantee that a specific output originated from a specific AI model.
**IP Protection:** The system uses model "fingerprints" that allow for verification without revealing the underlying model weights.
**Use Cases:** The technology is intended to prevent model swapping, verify third-party claims regarding AI-driven tasks, and ensure transparency in AI service delivery.
**Availability:** Technical specifications and source code are currently available on GitHub under an open-source license.
**Deployment Status:** The project is an ongoing research initiative with no current plans for integration into Anthropic’s commercial products.

title: Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 17:32 EST / NOVEMBER 03 2026

Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation

Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees.

Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company.

In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later.

Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July . Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease.

Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc.

Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor.

Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia

summary.tldr:
Generative media inference startup fal (formally Features & Labels Inc.) has raised $1.3 billion in a Series F funding round, bringing its valuation to $16 billion. The company, which provides a cloud platform for running image, video, and audio generation models via a unified API, plans to utilize the capital to expand its 185-person workforce and secure additional computing power. CEO Burkay Gur noted that the funding was necessitated by surging demand that forced the company to implement rate-limiting on its services during the summer.

Fal differentiates itself by post-training third-party models to improve inference speed, focusing heavily on video generation over the past year. The company operates under a business model that includes licensing fees and revenue-sharing agreements with model developers. While fal currently does not have immediate plans to pretrain its own foundation models, it has achieved an annualized revenue run rate exceeding $800 million. The company's valuation places it just behind competitor Fireworks AI, which reached a $17.5 billion valuation in July.

The Series F round was led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital, and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. This follows a $350 million Series E round in April at an $8 billion valuation, bringing the company's total capital raised to over $1.9 billion. Talia Goldberg of Bessemer Venture Partners will join the company's board of directors.
takeaways: **Funding & Valuation:** Raised $1.3 billion in Series F funding at a $16 billion valuation, with total lifetime funding exceeding $1.9 billion.
**Financial Performance:** Reported an annualized revenue run rate of over $800 million as of earlier this year.
**Operational Scale:** Employs 185 people and serves entertainment studios, advertising agencies, and game developers through a single API.
**Strategic Backing:** Nvidia participated in the round as a strategic investor; Bessemer Venture Partners led the round.
**Market Comparison:** Valuation is slightly lower than rival inference provider Fireworks AI, which is valued at $17.5 billion.

title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
author: Aditya Mehta
contentSnippet:
Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week .

In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets.

In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.

Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

Converted jet en

summary.tldr:
AI data center operators are increasingly deploying converted jet engines to bypass multi-year grid connection delays, according to reports from the New York Times. By utilizing turbines salvaged from retired aircraft and retrofitted to burn natural gas, companies can achieve operational status in approximately 24 months. This timeline contrasts sharply with traditional grid infrastructure, which the International Energy Agency notes can take up to seven years to deliver 100 megawatts of power in regions like Northern Virginia.

Major industry players are actively adopting this stopgap measure. Elon Musk’s xAI has installed eight ProEnergy-rebuilt GE jet turbines at its Colossus 2 facility in Memphis, Mississippi. Similarly, OpenAI is utilizing gas turbines at its Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, a project managed by Denver-based startup Crusoe. While Crusoe previously considered a $1.25 billion deal for 29 turbines from Boom Supersonic, it ultimately pivoted to an order for 13 ProEnergy units in April 2025. These deployments are being encouraged by the current U.S. administration as a means to circumvent infrastructure bottlenecks.

Despite the speed of deployment, these converted engines present significant trade-offs. They are less fuel-efficient and generate higher emissions than purpose-built power plant turbines. Industry experts suggest that as environmental regulations and efficiency standards tighten, these jet-engine-based power solutions may prove to be a short-term strategy rather than a permanent infrastructure fix.
takeaways: **Deployment Speed:** Converted jet engines allow data centers to become operational in 24 months, compared to the seven-year wait times for standard grid connections.
**xAI Implementation:** xAI has deployed eight ProEnergy-rebuilt GE jet turbines to support the Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, Mississippi.
**OpenAI/Crusoe Project:** OpenAI’s Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, utilizes gas turbines, with Crusoe ordering 13 ProEnergy units for the campus in April 2025.
**Failed Deal:** Crusoe canceled a $1.25 billion agreement to purchase 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic in September.
**Operational Risks:** Converted jet engines are less efficient and more polluting than conventional power plant turbines, potentially limiting their long-term viability.

title: Anthropic Releases FlashProve: Cryptographic Proofs That a Reply Came From Committed Weights
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has released FlashProve , an open-source research prototype for provable inference . FlashProve is a zkSNARK system from Anthropic that proves a reply came from a committed model. The proof reveals nothing about the model weights. On Llama 4 Maverick , a 400B mixture-of-experts model, it proves about 110 tokens/second on 1 H100. For developers, this targets a real gap: today you cannot check which model actually answered your API call. TL;DR Size: Proves a 400B MoE model (~17B active per token); context capped at 1,024 tokens per request. Runs on: Prover needs 1 H100 80 GB, 24 CPU cores and ~290 GB host RAM. Verifier runs on a CPU, no GPU. Performance: Orders of magnitude faster than prior open-source zkML systems on the same 400B model. Best: 110 tokens/second proving on 1 H100, with 18.78 MB proofs checked in 17 seconds. Worst: Proving costs ~70 to 95x the GPU time of plain vLLM inference. What problem does provable inference solve? A user querying a model cannot verify which model produced the response. A routing service could swap in a cheaper model . An attacker could tamper with the token stream. Judging from output quality alone is unreliable. Anthropic lists 4 use cases: Regulators could confirm hardware serves inference, supporting AI pacing rules. Labs could detect tampered inference servers. Users could verify text provenance. Regulators could enforce serving of approved models only. How does FlashProve work? FlashProve has a prover (the model provider) and a verifier (the user). It runs in 2 phases: Offline: The provider publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint binding one exact set of weights. This takes about 39 minutes and covers about 16 million requests. Online: For each request, the GPU produces a proof that the committed model produced those tokens. The proof system compiles an interactive oracle proof into a cryptographic proof using hash functions. Anthropic says this offers post-quantum security. It is the same family used by validity-proof L2 networks such as Starknet. Three engineering choices drive the speed. Prover work scales with the ~17B active parameters, not all 400B. Requests are proved in batches after the fact, like prefill. Weights stream from host memory, so a single 80 GB GPU suffices. How fast is it? Benchmarks Anthropic measured the public 4-bit Maverick weights on 1 H100 with 24 CPU cor

summary.tldr:
Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has introduced FlashProve, an open-source zkSNARK-based research prototype designed to provide cryptographic verification that a specific model generated a given response. By utilizing a commitment scheme, the system allows providers to prove that a reply originated from a specific set of model weights without revealing the weights themselves. This addresses a critical transparency gap in the AI supply chain, where users currently lack the ability to verify if an API provider has swapped a high-performance model for a cheaper, lower-quality alternative or if the token stream has been tampered with.

Technically, FlashProve is optimized for large-scale models, specifically demonstrating performance on the 400B parameter Llama 4 Maverick mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which utilizes approximately 17B active parameters per token. The system achieves a proving throughput of 110 tokens per second on a single H100 80GB GPU, with proofs sized at 18.78 MB that can be verified on a standard CPU in 17 seconds. While the proving process incurs a 70x to 95x GPU time overhead compared to standard vLLM inference, it utilizes post-quantum secure hash functions similar to those found in Starknet. The architecture relies on an offline phase—taking roughly 39 minutes to commit to 16 million requests—and an online phase where proofs are generated in batches.

FlashProve is positioned for use cases involving regulatory compliance, such as verifying that hardware is serving approved models, as well as enabling users to confirm text provenance and labs to detect tampered inference servers. The system requires significant host resources, including 24 CPU cores and 290 GB of host RAM, to manage the streaming of weights from host memory to the GPU, allowing the entire process to run on a single H100 node.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Achieves 110 tokens/second proving speed on a 400B MoE model using a single H100 80GB GPU.
**Resource Requirements:** Prover node requires 1 H100 GPU, 24 CPU cores, and approximately 290 GB of host RAM.
**Verification Efficiency:** Generates 18.78 MB proofs that are verifiable on a standard CPU in 17 seconds.
**Operational Overhead:** Proving costs are 70 to 95 times higher in GPU time compared to standard vLLM inference.
**Security Foundation:** Utilizes post-quantum secure cryptographic proofs based on interactive oracle proofs, similar to L2 validity-proof networks.

title: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA’s latest technical blog shows how to speed up mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on one DGX Spark . The test model is Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash , a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters. NVIDIA stacked three optimizations: a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. On all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change. So why is it relevant for Devs? DGX Spark is a desktop system, not a data center node. NVIDIA’s results show a 124B MoE serving single-user requests faster on that desk-side box. The technical post also shows where MoE decode time goes, and how to cut it. TL;DR Size: Ling-3.0-flash-fp4: 124B total, 5.1B active per token; 256K native context. Runs on: One NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory, 273 GB/s), batch size one. Performance: Three stacked optimizations lift GSM8K decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens/s. Best: +42.5% throughput and -24.5% mean latency, with accuracy flat (96.89% vs 96.82%). Lagging: Synthetic gains (+185.1%) shrink on GSM8K as MTP acceptance drops from 3.90 to 2.68. Why is MoE decoding on DGX Spark memory-bound? DGX Spark is NVIDIA’s desktop system built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. It offers 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Peak compute is up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4. NVIDIA rates it for inference on models up to 200B parameters. In the NVIDIA technical post , the NVIDIA team profiled Ling-3.0-flash-fp4 at batch size 1. Decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out, the MoE computation and the LM head that scores the vocabulary. That points to two levers: move fewer bytes per decode step, and generate more tokens per verification round. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe. It used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 LM-head path. On a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test, it ran at 27.71 ms per token (36.09 tokens per second). What are the 3 optimizations? 1. Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels: NVIDIA swapped FlashInfer’s MoE backend for Humming , an independent kernel library. Humming uses NVRTC to compile kernels at runtime for the actual matrix shapes, data types and GPU. That includes the narrow 768-wide expert layer. Each kernel compiles in seconds. title: Soniox STT v6 Adds Agent Text Input and Echo Filtering for Voice Agents
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Soniox has released Soniox STT v6 , the latest generation of its speech-to-text API. Soniox STT v6 is a speech-to-text model that reads what a voice agent says while hearing the caller. It uses that text to recognize short replies and to drop the agent’s own voice. The release ships as stt-rt-v6 for streaming and stt-async-v6 for files , across 60+ languages. TL;DR Size: Soniox STT v6 is a proprietary hosted model, no parameter count published. Runs on: Soniox cloud API only (WebSocket streaming and async REST). No self-hosted or on-device option disclosed. Performance: Soniox calls it “significantly” more accurate than v5, but publishes no v6 numbers yet. Best: Price. $0.12/hour streaming and $0.10/hour async, with diarization and language ID bundled. Worst: Zero independent v6 results. Its v5 predecessor scored 1.34% semantic WER on Pipecat, behind v4’s 1.25%. What problem does Soniox STT v6 solve? In a cascaded voice agent, STT usually hears only the caller. It never sees the question being answered. Short answers suffer most. In Soniox’s docs , “River Roast” becomes “River Road” and “a tow” becomes “a tour.” The second problem is echo. Agent audio leaks back through speakerphones and laptops, gets transcribed as user speech, and the agent interrupts itself. How does agent text input work? You enable it with one flag in the start request: "enable_agent_text_input": true . It is only available on stt-rt-v6 , not the async model. While the agent speaks, you stream its words on the same WebSocket as the caller’s audio. Each message is a small JSON frame: {"type": "agent_text", "text": "...", "end_of_segment": true} . Timing matters. Messages carry no timestamps, so the model places text where it arrives in the audio stream. Soniox recommends sending each piece 500 ms to 1 second before playback, paced by TTS timestamps. On barge-in, you flush what was already played, send end_of_segment: true , and drop the unplayed rest. The agent’s text never appears in the returned transcript. How does agent voice echo cancellation work? With agent text input on, v6 knows what the agent is saying. It uses that to separate leftover agent audio from caller speech and filter it out. It keeps listening during playback, so callers can still interrupt. It does not replace acoustic echo cancellation. It handles what your existing AEC leaves behind , so keep AEC on. What else cha

The release ships as stt-rt-v6 for streaming and stt-async-v6 for files , across 60+ languages. TL;DR Size: Soniox STT v6 is a proprietary hosted model, no parameter count published. Runs on: Soniox cloud API only (WebSocket streaming and async REST).

title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
author: Rohan Alexander
contentSnippet: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

title: Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood
author: Aisha Malik
contentSnippet:
Netflix announced on Tuesday that it’s rolling out a new “AI Discover” tab where users will be able to experiment with new ways to find their next watch. The first experimental feature launching under the tab will allow users to get recommendations based on what they’re currently in the mood for.

Users can choose from curated themes featuring clips from shows and movies, based on their mood, viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what’s new and trending. Themes include “something light,” “scare me,” “family movie night,” “quick watches,” and more.

The addition of the new tab suggests that Netflix wants to make its growing library easier to navigate while shifting discovery away from an experience where users are endlessly scrolling through titles toward a more personalized and AI-powered experience.

Netflix says AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer it’s been building that responds to what users tell the platform in real time and keeps learning.

Once users pick a theme, they’ll see matching recommendations. They also have the option to select more specific themes so they can keep searching until they find something they’re interested in, or choose the “something different” option to start over. Each title features a “Tune Your Recommendations” button beside “Play” and “My List” to allow users to save recommendations they like or exclude titles they don’t want suggested again.

“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix wrote in a blog post . “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”

Netflix describes AI Discover as its “test kitchen,” where it will “try out new recipes for discovery.” The company says users’ feedback will help it decide which features to keep or improve before bringing them over to the main Netflix experience.

AI Discover is starting to roll out in the U.S. to users who use Netflix in English on supported TVs. The company plans to bring the new tab to additional users in the coming weeks.

If users have access to the new feature, they’ll see a “Discover” button with a red gem icon and a “New” label in the top navigation bar

summary.tldr:
Netflix has introduced a new "AI Discover" tab, an experimental interface designed to replace traditional "endless scrolling" with a mood-based, interactive recommendation system. The feature is powered by a new intelligence layer that processes user input in real-time, allowing viewers to select curated themes such as "something light," "scare me," or "quick watches." Users can refine these suggestions through iterative prompts or by selecting a "something different" option to reset the discovery flow.

Beyond initial selection, the interface includes a "Tune Your Recommendations" button adjacent to the standard "Play" and "My List" controls. This allows users to explicitly save or exclude specific titles, providing a feedback loop that informs the underlying model. Netflix characterizes the AI Discover tab as a "test kitchen" for discovery features, where user engagement data will determine which tools are eventually integrated into the primary Netflix experience.

The feature is currently rolling out to English-language users in the U.S. on supported TV devices. Eligible users can access the tool via a "Discover" button marked with a red gem icon and a "New" label located in the top navigation bar.
takeaways: **Interface Access:** The feature is identified by a red gem icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar on supported TV devices.
**Feedback Mechanism:** A "Tune Your Recommendations" button allows users to manually save or exclude titles to influence future suggestions.
**Core Functionality:** The system uses a real-time intelligence layer to filter content based on mood, viewing preferences, time availability, and trending status.
**Deployment Scope:** Currently limited to U.S. users with English-language settings on supported TVs, with a broader rollout planned for the coming weeks.

title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected. Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles. Apple: * Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later. * Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment. When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

summary.tldr:
Apple has introduced new 'Audio Intelligence' features for the Apple Watch via the watchOS 27.3 developer beta. The update includes two primary tools: Siri Recap, which utilizes ambient listening to generate conversation summaries, and Live Rewind, which provides a 15-second text transcript of recent audio captured by the watch microphone. These features are designed to assist with memory recall and conversation engagement, with users able to trigger Live Rewind via a double-press of the Digital Crown.

Alongside the watchOS update, Apple released an iOS 27.3 developer beta featuring a redesigned Health app. This app includes a new 'Insights' tab for heart, sleep, and fitness data, a 'For You' section for personalized recommendations, and educational health content. The update expands language support to include global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

To address privacy concerns regarding always-on ambient listening, Apple published an Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview. The company claims raw audio is processed exclusively within dedicated hardware, is never saved as a file, and remains inaccessible to the operating system or third-party apps. Saved summaries and transcripts are end-to-end encrypted and synced across devices via iCloud for users with two-factor authentication and a device passcode.
takeaways: **Live Rewind Functionality:** Users can double-press the Digital Crown to view a 15-second text transcript of recent audio, which can be queried via Siri or saved to the Siri app.
**Siri Recap Architecture:** The feature automatically generates titles and key points from conversations, storing them in the Siri app for later review.
**Privacy Infrastructure:** Apple states that raw audio is processed in dedicated hardware and is not accessible to the OS or apps, with saved data protected by end-to-end encryption.
**Health App Redesign:** The iOS 27.3 beta introduces an Insights tab for daily health metrics and a For You section for personalized recommendations.

**Language Expansion:** The new features support 10 languages, including global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
author: Hayden Field
contentSnippet: In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.) Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities, including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said. Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and

summary.tldr:
OpenAI’s consumer product lead, Adam Fry, announced that ChatGPT’s search query volume has reached 20 percent of Google’s total search volume. OpenAI defines these search queries as inputs requiring a web search, excluding simple definitions or how-to explanations. While the specific methodology for calculating Google’s search volume was not disclosed, this metric highlights a significant shift in user behavior compared to Microsoft Bing, which held approximately 3 percent market share after over a decade of operation, as cited during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial.

OpenAI is positioning its search experience as an "Intelligent UI," moving toward an interactive, canvas-based interface rather than traditional link-based results. The company continues to rely on a combination of Microsoft Bing and its own in-house search index to power these queries. As OpenAI approaches a potential IPO in early 2025, it is actively expanding its advertising strategy. Fry noted that the introduction of sponsored product images has not caused user backlash, and the company is exploring ways to increase ad integration within the platform.
takeaways: **Search Volume:** ChatGPT search queries now reach 20 percent of the volume processed by Google.
**Market Context:** Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella previously testified that Bing held only 3 percent market share after more than 10 years of development.
**Ad Strategy:** OpenAI is transitioning from simple text/logo-based ads to sponsored product images, with leadership suggesting potential for further ad expansion.
**Interface Philosophy:** OpenAI describes its search evolution as an "Intelligent UI" or "canvas," focusing on visual and interactive responses rather than traditional search referrals.

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
author: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang
contentSnippet: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus 5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs 107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \117 for teleoperation in China and below 290 in labour alone in North America.

title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
author: Minsoo Cheong, Sungjoo Yoo
contentSnippet: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to 4.3times and 6.1times on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
