Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira . Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
author: Daxeshkumar Patel
contentSnippet: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content. title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
author: Giuseppe Zappia
contentSnippet: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)? The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as lo

summary.tldr:
Amazon Web Services has released a technical guide on using sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD) to optimize agentic AI applications hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI. The methodology addresses the high operational costs associated with multi-step agentic loops—where models perform iterative tasks like searching, reading, refining, and verifying—by transferring the behavioral capabilities of a large 'teacher' frontier model to a smaller, more cost-effective 'student' model.

SeqKD functions by using the teacher model to generate high-quality, multi-step task trajectories, which are then used as training data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the student model. This approach is specifically designed for API-only or closed-source teacher models, as it requires only the output text rather than access to internal logits or complex reinforcement learning infrastructure. The workflow detailed by AWS covers the generation of successful task trajectories, data encoding for SFT, execution on serverless infrastructure, and benchmarking the student model against held-out datasets to ensure performance parity.
takeaways: **Methodology:** SeqKD utilizes supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher-generated text outputs to train smaller student models without requiring access to teacher model logits.
**Operational Efficiency:** The approach targets the reduction of per-task costs in agentic loops, where multiple model calls are typically required for a single user request.
**Infrastructure:** The training process is designed to run on Amazon SageMaker AI, utilizing serverless infrastructure for the fine-tuning phase.
**Scope:** The technique is specifically applicable to closed or API-only frontier models where internal model weights or probability distributions are inaccessible.

title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Aishwarya Gavili
contentSnippet: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. Solution overview The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review. Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced a multi-agent engineering assistant architecture designed to automate the evidence-gathering process for aerospace component substitutions. By integrating Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the open-source Strands Agents SDK, the system aims to replace manual cross-referencing of datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records. The assistant is structured to ensure the human engineer remains the final decision-maker, with the AI responsible for retrieving data, scoring candidates, and drafting assessment documentation.

The architecture relies on a hybrid approach that separates deterministic logic from LLM-based reasoning. A central planner routes tasks to three specialist agents: a Catalog agent for searching, an Evaluation agent for scoring candidates against deterministic Python-based tolerance rules, and a Knowledge agent for grounding lifecycle claims in web data. The system utilizes Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings to extract information from engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts, addressing the limitations of text-only retrieval pipelines. The final output is a formal, repeatable evidence package intended for engineering review, rather than an autonomous decision-making process.
takeaways: **Core Technology Stack:** Utilizes Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings for visual data extraction, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for orchestration, and the Strands Agents SDK for multi-agent framework.

**Agent Specialization:** The system employs three distinct agents: a Catalog agent for search, an Evaluation agent for deterministic tolerance rule scoring, and a Knowledge agent for external web-based lifecycle verification.
**Deterministic Guardrails:** Engineering tolerance rules are implemented via Python code to ensure consistent, verifiable pass/flag verdicts that meet formal review standards.
**Human-in-the-loop Design:** The system is architected to draft assessments and assemble evidence packages, explicitly prohibiting the AI from approving component substitutions independently.

title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
author: Marek Klatowicz
contentSnippet: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. The challenge of triage overhead Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , exa

summary.tldr:
Circle K, which manages cloud-native infrastructure for over 17,200 retail locations across 27 countries, has implemented an agentic AI system on Amazon Bedrock to automate DevOps incident triage. By integrating this system into their existing Grafana-based monitoring stack, the company reduced mean incident triage time from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes, representing a 67–75 percent efficiency gain. The system replaces manual log correlation and service health checks with an automated process that delivers structured, actionable incident summaries directly to Slack.

The architecture utilizes Amazon Bedrock to provide foundation models via a single API, transitioning from an initial implementation using Amazon Bedrock Flows to the current Amazon Bedrock AgentCore framework. The system autonomously investigates alerts—such as container restarts, latency spikes, and failed deployments—by querying Amazon CloudWatch logs and correlating symptoms across the company's AWS-hosted point-of-sale, loyalty, and EV charging applications. This shift allows on-call engineers to bypass the initial investigative phase and proceed directly to remediation.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** Mean incident triage time reduced from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes.
**Efficiency Gain:** Achieved a 67–75 percent reduction in time spent on manual incident investigation.
**Infrastructure Scale:** Supports cloud-native operations for 17,200+ retail stores across 27 countries.

title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can ‘predict human behavior’
author: Ram Iyer
contentSnippet:
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?

Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.

“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.

“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added CTO and co-founder Ehud Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”

“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company us

summary.tldr:
Israeli startup 42AI has emerged from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding, developing what it terms a "behavioral world model" designed to predict human decision-making probabilities under volatile conditions. Founded by CEO Amit Gal-Or, CTO Ehud Ezra, and Chairman Amir Gal-Or, the company spent three years building the system by incorporating psychological research, neuroscience, genetics, and consultation from 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry laureate Dan Shechtman, alongside government and biobank datasets covering over 2 million people before expanding customer datasets to nearly 30 million.

The system utilizes a transformer-based world model fed by mathematical trait representations extracted from multi-channel user data, such as support calls, voice sentiment, onboarding metadata, and transaction history. A separate language model generates textual explanations for the predictions. In live deployments across 10 financial brokerages managing liquidity, hedging, and margin requirements, 42AI claims its system achieves an F1 score between 0.8 and 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume, alongside a 98% accuracy metric measuring whether trading flows fall within a predicted range. The startup operates on a business model combining flat fees and performance-percentage models, generating over seven figures in annual revenue.

Despite commercial deployment, 42AI acknowledges accuracy drops when situational context is missing—such as unobserved advice from peers—and faces ethical scrutiny regarding potential exploitation of profiled customer behavior. The company relies on internal ethics committees and regulatory compliance to address these concerns, while actively exploring expansion into gaming, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, and robotic human-intent modeling.
takeaways: **Funding and Backing:** 42AI raised $62.5 million in seed funding over a three-year period from the founders and Infinity Group, which was co-founded by chairman Amir Gal-Or.

**Model Architecture:** The system employs a transformer-based world model paired with a separate language model to generate explanations, processing behavioral traits derived from interactions like support calls, onboarding steps, and financial transactions.

**Performance Metrics:** The startup claims an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for forecasting trading direction and volume, and a 98% accuracy metric indicating whether trading flows fall within a predicted range.

**Dataset Scale:** Initial training incorporated psych assessments of thousands of individuals and government/biobank datasets exceeding 2 million people, which later expanded to customer datasets covering nearly 30 million people.

**Commercial Traction:** 42AI is deployed across 10 large financial brokerages for liquidity management and dynamic hedging, generating over seven figures in revenue under flat-fee or percentage-of-gain pricing models.

title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
author: Serdarcan Dilbaz
contentSnippet: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
author: YuJie Liu
contentSnippet: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
author: Shangziqi Zhao
contentSnippet: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.

In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
author: Zilu Zhang, Jing Bao, Lifeng Qiao, Sheng Xu
contentSnippet: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing.These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
author: Jiajie Jin
contentSnippet: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.

title: Dissecting Geometric Constraints in Grokking: Interaction-Dependent Acceleration in Modular Arithmetic
author: Zachary A. Hampton
contentSnippet: Spherical transformer configurations can accelerate grokking through simultaneous modifications of several model properties. The present study investigated the contributions of these modifications in the published Sphere+Fourier configuration using 960 controlled modular-arithmetic runs. A complete factorial analysis varied residual projection, readout weight normalization, logit scale, and weight decay. Across four matched settings with weight decay, the successful-run mean crossing times without projection were 8-37 times those observed with projection. However, residual projection was insufficient to induce grokking without additional interventions. Various other unprojected configurations also generalized. Since projection altered the magnitude entering the readout, these comparisons could not separate geometry from output scale. A separate 100-run fixed-horizon study demonstrated faster first crossing for the complete configuration across five train/test partitions. Faster crossing did not necessarily correspond to greater persistence over extended training. Control experiments demonstrated rapid grokking without Fourier initialization. Task and depth sweeps also identified conditions in which the configuration failed to reach the criterion by 50K epochs. Accordingly, the observed acceleration depended on interactions among the components and did not extend uniformly across the tested tasks or depths.

title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
author: Simon Willison AI

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
author: Affan Syed
contentSnippet: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight model

title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver
author: Jeong-gi Kwak, Andrea Tagliasacchi, Sho Kagami, Yuki Ono
contentSnippet: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how ``solved'' they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.

title: The agentic web is here
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
author: Yuxuan Du
contentSnippet: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. TL;DR Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b , with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported). Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results. Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it. What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology? It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. Here are the five jobs: Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models. Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage. Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API. Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. How does Auto Ontology work? The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. title: Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B With 45 Compiled GPU Layers That Run CUDA
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B . Developer Vixhal ( @TheVixhal ) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it. TL;DR Size: Qwen3.5-2B (24 layers) along with 45 compiled GPU layers, 69 in total. Context: 262,144 tokens (base model). Runs on: Apple silicon, an NVIDIA GPU or a CPU, with about 16 GB of free memory. No quantized build. Performance: Every launch in the developer’s runs was exact; text drift is a KL of about 7e-4. Best: The reference interpreter matched a real NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels. Worst: About 10 to 15 tokens per second on Apple MPS; Qwen-written CUDA passed 4 of 5. What is qwenGPU? qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight. How does a GPU fit inside model weights? The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs. The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell. That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post. The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. title: RLVR Sharpens the Pencil, Not the Mind
author: Shreeyam Bangera
contentSnippet: Models like DeepSeek-R1 made Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) famous: reward a model for correct answers and it gets dramatically better at reasoning without being taught how. The leading explanation is sharpening---that the base model already knows how to solve these problems and RLVR just makes it more likely to reach for its best solution paths. This has only ever been checked by comparing before and after training, never by watching what changes inside across it. We tracked OLMo-2-1B across all 13 training checkpoints on GSM8K. First-try accuracy climbs from 58.0% to 61.3%, but ask the model 256 times and solution coverage actually rises from 94.5% to 96.9%, proving the knowledge was already there. We then planted reasoning mistakes into problems and trained simple probes to detect them. Those probes held between AUROC 0.798 and 0.840 across all 13 checkpoints and 3 error types, a spread smaller than the confidence interval; the model never builds a sharper internal picture of what a reasoning mistake looks like. The one place we find real internal change is at the final answer token, where a probe distinguishing early from late checkpoints hits an AUROC of 0.93, while the same probe on the actual reasoning steps lands near chance. RLVR makes the model lead with its best thinking. It does not change what that thinking is.

title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
author: Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, Dongsheng Luo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chenjie Qiu , Boyan Xu , Shaobin Shi , Bingfeng Chen , Ruichu Cai , Dongsheng Luo

Abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

Notes: 13 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, and Dongsheng Luo introduced CLR-Bench (Curriculum of Latent Rules), a benchmark designed to evaluate whether self-evolving agents can learn hidden rules through feedback rather than simply memorizing exceptions. The benchmark consists of 20 chains across 10 data domains, where each level adds a hidden rule based on opaque labels representing real-world groupings, such as airline alliance members. The task provides a single example, followed by practice feedback identifying one member and one non-member, before testing the agent on unseen members and similar non-members.

Evaluation of six recent self-evolution methods revealed significant limitations: when using a certifying model, the best-performing agents gained only 5 points over frozen agents, failing to outperform raw practice history. These agents typically stored individual members in their state rather than identifying the underlying class name. However, providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points. When tested with the more capable GPT-6-Sol model, methods like ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet achieved 78% accuracy and solved 59-60% of single cells, demonstrating that the ability to learn from feedback is highly dependent on the underlying model's reasoning capabilities.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** CLR-Bench includes 20 chains across 10 distinct data domains to test rule-learning capabilities.
**Performance Gap:** Self-evolving agents using standard certifying models gained at most 5 points over frozen agents, underperforming compared to simple raw history retention.
**Instructional Impact:** Providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved agent performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points.
**Model Dependency:** Using the GPT-6-Sol model allowed ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet to reach 78% accuracy, significantly outperforming the certifying model baseline of 53%.

**State Behavior:** Agents frequently stored revealed members in their persistent state (75-98% of cases) but failed to identify or store the actual class name, indicating a reliance on list-building rather than rule generalization.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
author: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhifei Hu , Alexandra I. Cristea , Adel Bibi , Jialin Yu

Abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

summary.tldr: A new arXiv study (2610.40798v1) reveals that current web world models fail to ensure safety sufficiency despite generating plausible future predictions, scoring an alarming disconnect in 86.1% of evaluated scenarios. This exposes a critical gap in agentic architecture, proving that visual or textual plausibility does not equate to reliable risk mitigation for autonomous web agents.
takeaways: Evaluated 3,000 predictions across ten frozen open-source models in a rigorous matched human evaluation framework.
Demonstrates that an 86.1% failure rate in safety sufficiency occurs even when models output highly convincing, plausible future trajectories.
Shifts industry focus from generative visual/state prediction accuracy to explicit alignment and safety-bound verification layers.

title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
author: Nastaran Okati, Ricardo Olmedo, Moritz Hardt
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nastaran Okati , Ricardo Olmedo , Moritz Hardt

Abstract: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.

summary.tldr: A new research paper explores overcoming the computational hardness of computational arbitrage in AI model marketplaces. This breakthrough enables intermediaries to efficiently optimize inference purchasing across heterogeneous providers to maximize margins.
takeaways: Formalizes computational arbitrage as a mechanism to exploit cost and capability discrepancies across heterogeneous AI model providers.
Addresses the computational hardness barrier, transforming an intractable routing problem into a tractable operational strategy for inference intermediaries.
Shifts the market dynamics toward automated brokerages that sit between end-users and base model providers to optimize price-performance dynamically.

title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
author: Fengji Jing, Guy Laban
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fengji Jing , Guy Laban

Abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fengji Jing and Guy Laban have introduced a new methodology for evaluating multimodal speech emotion recognition (SER) in audio-capable Large Language Models (LLMs) by quantifying 'incongruence'—the discrepancy between textual content and vocal delivery. By mapping both modalities into a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space, the authors developed a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model. This metric was validated against human judgment and tested across three distinct datasets: eNTERFACE'05 (acted), MELD (conversational), and CMU-MOSEI (spontaneous).

The study reveals that when audio is present, incongruence significantly increases the probability of classification error in LLMs, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance. Notably, this behavior contrasts with supervised classifiers trained on identical features, which do not exhibit the same performance degradation. This suggests that the failure point is specific to how LLMs integrate multimodal evidence rather than an inherent limitation of the input signals. The researchers found that text-only effects were inconsistent, as swapping the underlying transcript-reading model could reverse performance trends, whereas their proposed incongruence score remained a robust predictor of error across all tested corpora.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Developed a label-free, continuous incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model in a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space.

**Performance Impact:** Incongruence between text and audio channels consistently increases the odds of error in audio-capable LLMs across all three evaluated datasets (eNTERFACE'05, MELD, CMU-MOSEI).
**Comparative Finding:** Supervised classifiers trained on the same features perform differently than LLMs, indicating the issue lies in the LLM's multimodal evidence integration architecture.
**Robustness:** The proposed incongruence score outperformed six simpler alternatives as the only metric capable of predicting errors across all three corpora without requiring emotion labels.
**Resource Availability:** The authors have released the source code, data tables, and prompts used in the study.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
author: Ayana Hussain, Nicholas Vincent
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ayana Hussain , Nicholas Vincent

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

summary.tldr: A new exploratory case study investigates the dual-use risks of consumer large language models like ChatGPT functioning as surveillance assistants. The research highlights growing concerns over how widely accessible LLM capabilities can be co-opted for targeted monitoring and tactical digital tracking.
takeaways: The study evaluates how easily general-purpose consumer LLMs can generate actionable guidance for digital and physical surveillance operations.
Widespread public access to advanced code and text generation lowers the barrier to entry for building scalable surveillance infrastructure.
Enterprise and research communities must re-evaluate safety guardrails against dual-use exploitation in automated monitoring contexts.

title: Does Recursive Knowledge Construction Help Agents Verify Consensus Claims in Science?
author: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
contentSnippet:
Authors: Lun Ai , Yu-Heng Wu , Jonathan Schaul , Leonie Küchenhoff , Denes Turei , Francesco Carli , Fabio Petroni , Aurelien Dugourd , Julio Saez-Rodriguez

Abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Lun Ai and Julio Saez-Rodriguez have introduced ProClaim, a framework designed to evaluate recursive knowledge construction in scientific agents. The study focuses on two primary design axes: the structure of the evidence state and the mechanism controlling the recursion (the 'judge'). To facilitate this, the team developed ProClaim-eval, a new benchmark dataset containing 718 scientific claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy, each labeled with 'SUPPORT' or 'REFUTE' ground truth derived from expert-curated databases.

Technically, ProClaim maintains an evidence state external to the model's context window, allowing for modular testing of design choices. Experimental results demonstrate that maintaining an external, structured evidence state outperforms standard in-context accumulation methods. Furthermore, the study finds that a trained judge—specifically one trained separately from the evaluation set—consistently outperforms fixed-round stopping mechanisms. When compared against general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks in the top three, showing significant performance advantages in verifying consensus scientific claims.

Performance analysis indicates that the trained judge matches the efficacy of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and exceeds that of Claude 3.5 Haiku on three of the five dataset subsets. The authors conclude that decoupling the evidence state from the model's context is a critical architectural requirement for reliable scientific verification, providing a more robust alternative to end-to-end agent evaluation without ground truth.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** ProClaim-eval consists of 718 scientific claims with gold-standard labels across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
**Architectural Advantage:** Storing evidence outside the model's context window yields higher verification accuracy compared to traditional in-context accumulation.
**Judge Performance:** A separately trained judge achieves parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and outperforms Claude 3.5 Haiku on 60% of the tested scientific domains.
**System Ranking:** ProClaim ranks among the top three systems for consensus claim verification, significantly outperforming general-purpose agent harnesses.
**Design Findings:** The study confirms that the specific content stored in the evidence state and the use of a trained judge are the primary drivers of verification success.

title: Towards Portable Specification of the Agent Harness
author: Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, Luciano Floridi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nicolas Gertler , Claudio Novelli , Luciano Floridi

Abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

summary.tldr:
Authors Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, and Luciano Floridi propose a standardized, portable specification framework for 'agent harnesses'—the infrastructure surrounding large language models that dictates their operational capabilities and failure modes. The authors argue that current documentation standards, such as model cards and agent cards, fail to capture the dynamic nature of these harnesses, which can cause multi-fold variations in performance benchmarks for identical models.

The proposed framework decomposes the harness into eight distinct functional components, enabling researchers to record and version the specific configuration under which a model operates. This is critical because agent harnesses are not static; they can evolve between releases, across different runs, and even during a single execution if an agent modifies its own tools or configuration. The authors emphasize that this documentation is essential for security, as a significant portion of an agent's attack surface is embedded within the harness rather than the model weights themselves. While emerging AI regulations mandate documentation for covered systems, the authors note that current legal frameworks do not yet require the granular, versioned harness records necessary for reproducibility and safety.
takeaways: **Functional Decomposition:** The framework categorizes the agent harness into eight distinct functional components to allow for cross-system comparison.
**Performance Variance:** The authors identify that identical models can exhibit multi-fold differences in benchmark scores depending on the specific harness configuration used.
**Security Implications:** A primary motivation for the framework is that the harness constitutes a major portion of an agent's attack surface, which is currently under-documented.
**Regulatory Gap:** Existing AI laws impose documentation duties but fail to prescribe the specific, versioned harness records required to track configuration changes within or between runs.
